items.title: HM could form new procedural but not episodic memories
items.claim: Henry Molaison (HM) had bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in 1953 for severe epilepsy. After the operation:

options.text: He had no memory of any kind
He could not form new conscious (declarative) memories but could acquire procedural skills like mirror-tracing — improving with practice while denying ever having done the task
He recovered fully within a year
He became a famous psychologist himself

items.reveal:
Brenda Milner began studying HM in 1955. Her 1962 paper documented procedural learning despite dense anterograde amnesia. HM died in 2008; his identity was revealed posthumously. His brain was sliced into 2,401 sections (Annese et al. 2014) and photographed, available online.

His case established that medial temporal lobe (especially hippocampus) is essential for new declarative memory formation but not for procedural learning. Suzanne Corkin worked with HM for 46 years.
items.why: Single-case neuropsychology can produce findings that constrain theories of normal cognition for generations. The dissociation between memory systems was visible in one patient.

items.title: Flow requires challenge matching skill
items.claim: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's flow research (1975 onwards) identified conditions for the optimal experience. What characterises flow?

options.text: Challenge matched to skill (slightly stretching), clear goals, immediate feedback, deep concentration, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, time distortion

items.reveal:
Csikszentmihalyi's Experience Sampling Method (ESM, 1975) gave participants pagers; when paged at random they noted what they were doing and how they felt. The pattern: deep enjoyment occurred when skill and challenge were both high.

Too little challenge → boredom; too much → anxiety. Sports psychology uses flow frameworks for performance preparation. Critics (Engeser 2012) note flow may be more available in certain activity types and that measurement post-hoc is suspect.
items.why: Flow describes a measurable state but doesn't make it easy to engineer. The conditions can be designed for; the experience can't be commanded.

items.title: What we know about Little Albert
items.claim: John Watson and Rosalie Rayner's 1920 'Little Albert' study conditioned an infant to fear a white rat. What is now believed about the child's identity?

options.text: His identity was always public knowledge
Later researchers proposed identifications but no consensus exists
He grew up to become a famous psychologist
Records confirm he kept the conditioned fear for life

items.reveal:
Beck, Levinson and Irons (2009) proposed Douglas Merritte; Powell et al. (2014) proposed William Barger. The case remains unresolved.

The study itself would not meet modern ethical standards for research with infants.
items.why: Ethical reviews now prevent such studies. Their existence in the historical record shapes how we teach research ethics today.
